units: the writer explains what made her get up very early
an observing club had reported a passage of a celestial body
the clear sky decided her to take her telescope along
she drove for a good while before reaching the site
the planet passed very close to the lunar disk and was then hidden
the steady air made the image very sharp
she made out details she cannot reach from home
the cold slowed the instrument down as it settled to temperature
she invites her correspondent to come along the following night
text: You asked what dragged me out of bed before sunrise, so here is the whole story. The observing club had put out word about a close pass, and since the forecast promised a perfectly clean sky, I loaded the telescope into the back of the car. That meant a long stretch of dark driving and thoroughly frozen fingers, but what a sight it turned out to be. The planet slid right up against the edge of our own moon, then blinked out behind it, no fade and no warning. The air held perfectly still that night, so the view hardly wobbled at all and I picked out details I never manage from the balcony at home. The cold worked against me as well, since the tube took forever to settle, and I stood there breathing into my gloves while I waited. Come out with me tomorrow night and you will see the difference right away.

units: the interview deals with the crowding of the near orbits
craft that no longer work keep circling the globe once their mission ends
a collision produces a swarm of fragments
a tiny impact can puncture a tank
a tiny impact can tear off a receiving element
the specialist calls for a planned descent built in from the design stage
she also proposes catching the fragments already up there with a net or a harpoon
the captured debris would be steered into a controlled fall at sea
she judges the answer workable only if the operators adopt one shared rule
text: Should the crowding of the near orbits worry us? The engineer we spoke with does not hedge for a moment. Craft that stopped working long ago keep circling the globe well past the end of their missions, and every crash breeds a whole swarm of fragments. What does that mean for a satellite still in service? A nick no bigger than a grain can open a tank or strip an antenna clean off. So what does she want done about it? First, a planned descent, built into the design and paid for up front. Second, a sweep for the pieces already flying up there, snagged by net or harpoon and then steered down into a controlled fall at sea. Is any of that realistic? She thinks so, but only if the operators sign up to one shared rule and hold to it. Without that, each of them shoves the cost onto the next.

units: the keeper of the dome asks the narrator which he prefers between looking directly and recording
the narrator admits he cannot choose
she describes the human gaze as a brief act that leaves no trace
she describes the recording device as a tool that stacks moments
this stacking brings out what is too faint for the eye
the narrator objects that a drawing keeps something of feeling
she grants that a sketch holds the memory of an evening
she states that a raw image tells nothing on its own
she concludes that taking a picture means handing over one's memory
text: The woman who keeps the dome asked me one evening which I liked better, the eye or the sensor. I told her honestly that I could never manage to choose. So she set the two of them side by side for me. The eye, she said, grabs a moment the way a hand grabs a stone from a riverbed, quick and leaving nothing behind. The sensor waits instead. It stacks moment upon moment until whatever is far too faint to see finally shows itself. I argued back that a drawing holds a warmth no machine ever gets anywhere near. She smiled and gave me that one without a fight. A sketch carries a whole evening inside it, she said, while a raw frame carries nothing at all. Then came the line I keep coming back to. Looking is remembering with your own eyes. Taking a picture is handing your memory over to a machine.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the history of sky watching falls into families of instruments
the earliest tools rested on measuring angles with the naked eye
those tools leaned on tables copied out by hand
the lens telescope came next
the lens telescope suffers from a defect of color
the mirror removed that defect but makes the instrument heavier
the mirror made very large apertures possible
the sensitive plate gave access to bodies invisible to the eye
electronic sensors and antennas carried observation beyond visible light
each family of instruments inherited the methods of the one before it
text: The story of sky watching breaks into families of instruments, each with its own habits. The earliest tools measured angles with the naked eye and leaned on tables copied out by hand, generation after generation. The lens telescope came next. It shut the view inside a closed barrel, yet it never shook off a stubborn colored fringe. The mirror cleared that fringe away, at the cost of far more weight to swing, and it opened the door to apertures ground glass could never reach. The sensitive plate followed, reaching bodies far too faint for any retina. Then came electronic sensors and linked antennas, which carried the work out past visible light altogether. No family ever drove out the one before it. Each inherited the older ways of measuring, the old catalogs, and often the old mistakes.

units: a star forms from a cloud of cold gas that collapses
the contraction heats the center until fusion starts
fusion halts the collapse of the cloud
a long stable period follows with steady burning of the fuel
when the fuel runs out the envelope swells and the surface cools
the outer layers scatter and enrich the surrounding medium with heavy elements
a dense core is left at the center and cools without end
the most massive bodies end in an explosion
the blast from that explosion squeezes the neighboring clouds and sets off new births there
text: A star begins inside a cold cloud of gas that slowly gives way under its own weight. As the cloud draws inward, its core heats until fusion catches, and that fresh push outward halts the collapse for good. A long and even stretch follows, with the star working through its fuel at a thoroughly steady pace. Once the supply runs thin, the outer envelope swells enormously while the surface cools, and the whole body turns vast and reddish. Those outer layers eventually drift off into the surrounding space, seeding the medium around them with heavy elements. What stays behind is a dense, hot core that goes on cooling with no end in sight. The heaviest bodies take a rougher road and finish in an explosion whose blast squeezes the clouds nearby, where a fresh generation of stars begins to take shape.

units: an amateur left his listening station recording while he was away
a power cut threw the clock of the station off
the files piled up with no date to place them by
the amateur nearly deleted everything
he opened the last file and heard a short repeated signal in it
he sent the trace to a university observatory
a researcher identified an onboard transmitter that was believed dead
that craft spoke only when its panels caught the sunlight at a precise angle
the clock going wrong had shifted the listening runs into the one favorable window
text: A radio hobbyist made a habit of leaving his listening station running while he was away from home. A power cut knocked the clock out, so the recordings stacked up with nothing at all to date them by, and he came close to wiping the whole lot. On a whim he opened the last file anyway, and there it was, a short pulse returning at a perfectly steady beat. He had no idea what he was hearing, so he passed the trace along to a university observatory. A researcher there recognized the signature of an onboard transmitter that everyone had written off ages ago. Starved of power, the craft spoke up only when its panels caught the sunlight at one narrow angle. The broken clock had shifted his listening runs and dropped them straight into the one window where the thing had anything to say.

units: blurred images most often come from the setting of the mirrors and not from the sky
the instrument must be taken outside half an hour before observing
the heat held inside the tube spoils the image
the eyepiece is replaced by a pierced cap to check the centering
through that cap one should see circles nested in one another
an off center is corrected with the screws of the mirror at the back
the screws must never be tightened all the way
a bright star is then aimed at and thrown out of focus to give a ring
an uneven ring is put right by an eighth of a turn of the screw concerned
text: Fresh telescope out of the box, mushy images, and you are ready to quit? Nine times out of ten the mirrors are out of alignment and the sky is entirely innocent. Here is the routine. Set the instrument outside a good half hour before you plan to observe, or the heat trapped inside the tube will smear everything. Pull the eyepiece, drop a cap with a small hole in it into the focuser, and look through. You want circles nested neatly inside one another. If the middle sits off to one side, work the screws behind the rear mirror in tiny nudges, and never crank one down tight. Replace the eyepiece, aim at a bright star and throw it slightly out of focus until a ring appears. That ring should look even the whole way around. If it bunches up on one side, back the matching screw off by an eighth of a turn, no more.

units: a further receiving array is being built on an arid plateau
the engineers compare this worksite to an observatory placed outside the atmosphere
both installations aim at the same bodies
the installation on the ground can be extended and repaired piece by piece
the craft in orbit has to work without any human hand
the installation on the ground is hampered by the air that blurs the signals
the craft in orbit has vacuum in front of its shell
the installation on the ground enjoys plentiful electric power
the craft in orbit has to save every last store of energy
those in charge hold that the two approaches complete each other
text: Out on the dry plateau where the latest receiving array is going up, the engineers like to set their worksite against an observatory launched clear of the atmosphere. Both of them chase exactly the same bodies, and there the resemblance ends. The array on the ground can be stretched, patched and swapped out piece by piece. The orbiting craft has to work the first time, since no technician will ever climb up there to tighten a bolt. The array on the ground fights the air, which smears the very signals it wants. Its rival has nothing but vacuum in front of its shell. Power, on the other hand, runs freely into the plateau site, while the craft overhead counts every last scrap of energy it holds. The people running the project insist that the two answers fit together rather neatly.

units: the dome seen from the road looks like a pale pebble set on a ridge
its open slit lets an icy draft inside
the bare concrete floor inside throws back the sound of steps
the tube of the instrument leans toward the opening
the tube swings round with a dull unbroken sound
wooden drawers hold colored filters and wrapped eyepieces
an electrical panel blinks above the drawers
the sky outside is free of haze
one makes out a milky trail, a low reddish body and a satellite crossing the field
text: From the road that climbs the hill, the dome looks like a pale pebble that someone set down on the ridge. Its slit stands open like a heavy lid and lets an icy draft slide inside. The floor within is bare gray concrete, and it throws back the sound of every single step you take. The great tube of the instrument leans toward the opening and swings slowly around with a low, steady growl. Along the wall run wooden drawers where colored filters sleep beside eyepieces wrapped in cloth. An electrical panel blinks above them, on and off, on and off, all night long. Outside there is not a shred of haze anywhere in sight. A milky trail spills across the vault overhead, a reddish body sits low over the horizon, and the thread of a satellite drifts silently from one edge of the field to the other.

units: at first the sky surveys belonged to the team that had obtained them
that ownership shocked nobody because instruments were scarce
digital sensors produced volumes of measurements no single team could handle
open archives took hold because of those volumes
the present difficulty lies in sorting the data rather than in collecting it
the author holds that funding an instrument without funding the use of its data makes no sense
he asks that a fixed share of every program go to archiving
he also asks for funding of calibration and of public analysis tools
without that the measurements piled up will never be put to use
text: The case makes the most sense told in the order it grew. At the start, a sky survey belonged to the team that had taken it, and nobody objected, since plates were scarce and instruments scarcer still. Then digital sensors began pouring out measurements in volumes that no single team could ever work through, and open archives took hold almost without argument. That brings us to now, when the hard part is no longer gathering the data but sifting through it. My position fits into one line. Funding an instrument and not funding the use of its data is digging a well and buying no bucket. Agencies ought to set aside a fixed share of every program for archiving, for calibration and for analysis tools that anyone can pick up. Otherwise we pile up measurements no one will ever look at.
